title: TB5-02345
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Nigeria, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) rejecting her claim for refugee protection. She has not submitted new evidence in support of this appeal. The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and substitute its own determination that she is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, or refer the matter back to the RPD for redetermination.
Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.

The Appellant alleged before the RPD that she has a fear of abuse and possibly death by her ex-common-law partner. The Appellant and XXXX started living together in 2000. The first few years of the relationship were "heaven". However, XXXX became abusive after approximately ten years because the Appellant had not gotten pregnant. The Appellant went to her Pastor for prayer and counseling. The Pastor spoke to XXXX who promised to change his behaviour and stop drinking. In 2013, the Appellant and XXXX travelled to Mexico on vacation. The Appellant was happy that things were normal again.

During XXXX 2013, XXXX beat the Appellant. The Appellant went to her family doctor who suggested she report the abuse to the police. The police told the Appellant to return home. XXXX beat the Appellant worse than ever before for reporting him to the police.
In XXXX 2014, the Appellant attempted to leave XXXX, but he forced her to return.

In XXXX 2014, the Appellant's sister reported XXXX to the police in XXXX. A few days later, XXXX uncle, a XXXX police officer, informed XXXX the Appellant had reported him to the police. XXXX beat the Appellant with a belt and threatened to kill her if she dared to embarrass him again. He also cut the Appellant's arm with a knife. The next day, the Appellant went to the doctor and then went to see her Pastor. In XXXX, the Pastor called to inform the Appellant that he had made arrangements for her to go to Bayelsea. After one month, the police were looking for the Appellant in Bayelsea. That night, the Appellant fled to Lagos, as instructed by her sister XXXX.
XXXX knew an agent who helped the Appellant apply for an American visa using fraudulent documents. On or about XXXX XXXX, 2014, the Appellant travelled to the United States (US).

On or about XXXX XXXX, 2014, the Appellant travelled to Canada. The Appellant initiated this claim for protection soon afterwards. The Appellant alleges XXXX will beat, rape, and kill her if she is returned to Nigeria.

The Appellant's refugee claim was heard on February 2, 2015. In a decision of February 25, 2015, the RPD rejected the claim, finding that there was no serious possibility that the Appellant would be persecuted in Nigeria, or that she would be subjected personally to danger of torture, or face a risk to her life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment. RPD's Findings

The RPD in its Reasons found: a) The Appellant has a viable internal flight alternative in Lagos; b) The Appellant did not adequately explain her failure to make a claim in the United States (US); and c) The Appellant was lacking in credibility.

The Appellant submits the following issues: a) The RPD based its findings on peripheral issues; b) The RPD did not consider the Gender Guidelines1 in its analysis; c) The RPD erred in its assessment of the internal flight alternative (IFA); and d) The RPD failed to address relevant evidence in its decision.

The RAD finds that the recent Federal Court decision, in Huruglica,2 provides the RAD with guidance in relation to the appropriate standard that must be applied by the RAD to decisions of the RPD. Justice Phelan states in paragraphs 54 and 55 of the foregoing decision: [54] Having concluded that the RAD erred in reviewing the RPD's decision on the standard of reasonableness, I have further concluded that for the reasons above, the RAD is required to conduct a hybrid appeal. It must review all aspects of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the claimant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Where its assessment departs from that of the RPD, the RAD must substitute its own decision. [55] In conducting its assessment, it can recognize and respect the conclusion of the RPD on such issues as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching such a conclusion but it is not restricted, as an appellate court is, to intervening on facts only where there is an "overriding and palpable error".

While there has been some conflict in the case law from the Federal Court regarding the standard of review to be applied by the RAD when reviewing RPD decisions, Justice Martineau, in Alyafi,3 has said that, in the face of this conflict, the Federal Court should allow the RAD to apply either approach as long as the question of the scope of the appellate review of the RPD's decisions has not been settled by a final judgment by the Federal Court of Appeal or the Supreme Court of Canada.

Accordingly, the RAD will conduct its own assessment of the RPD's decision and come to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. Deference will be afforded to the credibility findings of the RPD or to other findings where the RPD has a particular advantage in reaching its conclusions. New Evidence

The Appellant did not submit new evidence in this appeal. She did submit a sworn affidavit, which attempts to add information and explain aspects of her testimony during the RPD hearing, which the RAD finds is not admissible as new evidence in this appeal. The RAD further notes that it improperly contains an argument which would be more appropriate in the memorandum of law, as an affidavit is supposed to be a sworn statement as to facts.

For the reasons that follow, in this case the RAD can confirm the RPD's determination based on the availability of an IFA in Nigeria. The issue was fully canvassed at the RPD hearing, and the Appellant made submissions with respect to it. Furthermore, in making a determination on the viability of an IFA, the RAD will review and assess the credibility findings made by the RPD, which have applicability to this determination. Basis of Claim (BoC) Narrative and Testimonial Inconsistencies
paragraphs.heading_before: ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

paragraphs.text: The RPD reviewed a series of situations where the Appellant's BoC narrative was inconsistent with her testimony during the hearing. The RPD found these inconsistencies detracted from the credibility of the Appellant's allegations. The Appellant submits that the negative credibility findings are premised on implausibility and conjecture. The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument in this issue for the reasons that follow. The XXXX 2013 Assault

The Appellant further submits that the RPD impugned her credibility on what amounted to "a memory test". The RAD in its review of the record as well as the audio recording of the hearing notes that counsel for the Appellant led the questioning during the hearing as an accommodation in consideration of the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines.

The Appellant was asked a series of questions based on her allegation of assault by her common-law spouse on XXXX XXXX, 2010. The Appellant in her testimony described that immediately following the assault, someone took her on a bicycle to a hospital where the doctor treated her, prescribed medication and suggested she contact the police. The Appellant then testified that she attended the police station. The RPD explained to the Appellant that the description in her BoC narrative differed greatly from her testimony. The Appellant was asked to explain why there was such an inconsistency. The Appellant did not address the question as put to her.

The RAD finds this contradiction especially troublesome. Counsel for the Appellant in leading the questioning, had structured much of his inquiry around a review of the Appellant's BoC narrative. The RAD notes that, in its review of the audio recording of the hearing, Appellant's counsel had reviewed this same episode shortly before the RPD inquiry. Although the Appellant argues that the questions of the RPD form a memory test, the RAD finds its review of the record indicates the Appellant provided testimony that directed the inquiry. The RAD recalls the words of the Federal Court Trial Division's decision in Castroman,4 wherein it was stated: A primary way of testing credibility is by comparing what is contained in the claimant's PIF narrative and his testimony at his hearing.

The RAD finds the Appellant failed to provide a reasonable explanation for this inconsistency and notes this inconsistency relates to a central component of her claim. The RAD finds the Appellant's testimony in respect of her alleged assaults by her common-law spouse lacking in credibility. The Counselling Sessions

The RPD found the Appellant's testimony in respect of the counselling sessions provided to herself and her common-law partner by her pastor to be inconsistent with the content of her BoC narrative and documentation from the pastor. The Appellant testified that she was unable to remember when the counselling took place and that her common-law spouse had only attended one session, and she continued to attend the sessions alone. The RPD noted for the Appellant that her BoC narrative provided details about her common-law spouse attending as well as the promises he made during the sessions. The RPD further explained to the Appellant that the letter from her pastor described providing both counselling and advisory roles to both of them. The Appellant provided no salient explanation for the inconsistency. The RAD finds the Appellant's inconsistent testimony in this situation detracts from the credibility of her allegations.

The RAD in its review of the Appellant's evidence as well as her testimony finds it supports the finding of the RPD in respect of the BoC omissions, and the Argument of the Appellant must fail. The Chairperson's Gender Guidelines

The Appellant submits that the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines were not applied appropriately in this claim and that the RPD only paid lip service to such consideration. The RAD is not persuaded by the Appellant's argument in this regard.

The RAD notes that, in its review of the RPD's Reasons, the RPD did specifically address the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines5 in paragraph nine of its Reasons. The RAD, in its review of the record, notes that it finds the RPD in its decision adequately applied the principles enshrined in them. The RAD finds that the Appellant's argument is without merit. The Psychological Report

The RPD assessed the psychological report6 submitted in evidence and assigned it little evidentiary weight based on its content and the lack of credibility demonstrated by the Appellant. The Appellant submits that the RPD on several occasions found the Appellant was evasive in her answers and it did not show how it had considered the report and the Gender Guidelines in its decision. The RAD is not persuaded by the argument of the Appellant in this issue.

The RAD notes a review of the record as described above confirms that the RPD addressed aspects of the Appellant's psychological report during the hearing. The RPD's Reasons address the diagnosis provided by Dr. XXXX as well as inconsistencies in this report in respect of the allegations presented by the Appellant at the hearing.

The RAD has reviewed and considered the report, which indicates the assessment consisted of a clinical impression based upon a sixty-minute interview, with no recorded clinical testing. Dr. XXXX clinical impression is that the female Appellant suffers from a stress or related disorder with prolonged duration, which will require treatment. The conclusion reached by the clinician is that treatment and guaranteed freedom from the threat of removal to Nigeria will result in recovery. He also notes that it will be impossible for the Appellant to feel safe anywhere in Nigeria, but offers no explanation of how he has come to these opinions. Dr. XXXX also states that the Appellant's condition will deteriorate if returned to Nigeria, but he again fails to state on what medical basis he has come to this opinion. Without an explanation of the clinical basis on which these opinions were formed, the RAD finds that Dr. XXXX opinions amount to mere speculation.

The RAD also finds that the psychological opinion contained in Dr. XXXX report was largely formulated on the Appellant's self-report rather than on independent clinical studies. The RAD further finds the Appellant has not provided persuasive evidence that she is unable to obtain the psychological treatment recommended by Dr. XXXX in the IFA location. The RAD finds it cannot give the report weight in offsetting the Appellant's testimonial inconsistencies during the hearing or in assessing the viability of the IFA.7 The RAD agrees with the finding of the RPD in this matter.

The RAD notes the Appellant in her submission beyond the statement about the psychological report did not identify any additional specific instances where she felt the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines were not applied. The RAD reviewed the record as well as the audio recording of the hearing and notes that the RPD, in its Reasons,8 addressed the application of the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines. The RAD notes the record indicates the RPD at the outset of the hearing discusses with counsel for the Appellant the findings of the psychologist's report and suggests accommodations they might make for the Appellant during the hearing. The RAD further notes the RPD utilized "reverse order of questioning" as one of the accommodations in this claim. Counsel for the Appellant led the questioning and the RPD followed the line of questioning initiated by her counsel. The RAD further finds its review of the audio recording of the hearing confirms that the Appellant was dealt with professionally without any indication of an insensitive approach from the RPD. The RAD finds the Appellant's argument in this instance is without merit. Internal Flight Alternative (IFA)

The RPD found that the Appellant had a viable IFA in Lagos. The Appellant submits that the RPD's credibility findings are in error and the IFA finding cannot be upheld. Alternatively, the Appellant argues that the RPD did not apply the proper test to the case at hand. The RAD is not persuaded by the arguments of the Appellant.

In assessing an IFA, the RPD must apply a two-pronged test cited in Rasaratnam9 suitably modified to take account of section 97 of the IRPA. 1) the Board must be satisfied on a balance of probabilities that there is no serious possibility of the claimant being persecuted in the part of the country to which it finds an IFA exists and/or the claimant would not be personally subject to a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture in the IFA. 2) moreover, the conditions in the part of the country considered to be an IFA must be such that it would not be unreasonable, in all the circumstances, including those particular to the claim, for him to seek refuge there.

Both prongs must be satisfied to find that the claimant has an IFA. The burden of proof rests with the Appellant to show that he does not have an IFA. The finding of an IFA must be based on a distinct evaluation of a region for that purpose taking into account the Appellant's identity. An IFA must be a realistic and attainable option. An Appellant cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in traveling there or staying there.10

The RAD finds that there is a reasonable and viable internal flight alternative available to the Appellant in Lagos. The RAD notes that the Nigerian constitution provides for the right to travel within Nigeria. The Police in Nigeria and the Uncle of the Common-law Spouse

The RPD in its Reasons concluded that the Appellant had not provided documentation to support any interaction with the police in Nigeria as well as any documentation to support the identity of the uncle of her common-law spouse. The Appellant submits the Appellant has provided evidence showing that she would not be free from persecution anywhere in Nigeria because the police refuse to protect her. The RAD is not persuaded by this argument.

The Appellant testified that she fears her common-law spouse and that his uncle is an XXXX police officer in Benin City. She further alleges her common-law spouse will find her anywhere in Nigeria, and she testified that she could not move to another city as her common-law spouse will be able to find her. The Appellant has further testified that she has reported her common-law spouse to the police at various police stations. The RAD's review of the record confirms the Appellant's sister (XXXX) assisted her with a report to the police on one of these occasions and that she later witnessed the Appellant's confrontation with the uncle. The Appellant was confronted by the RPD as to whether she had any evidence about contacting the police or the identity of the "uncle". The Appellant responded in the negative. When asked specifically about providing an affidavit from her sister, the Appellant replied, "I did not know this would be needed".

The RAD finds that the Appellant did not offer persuasive evidence that she had approached the police or that her common-law spouse's uncle exists and has the influence she alleges. This issue was fully explored in the RPD hearing. Given the Appellant's allegations that she had contacted the police as well as the alleged profile of the uncle and his influence in this claim, it is reasonable to expect that the Appellant would have been able to tender some documentation to verify these allegations.

The RAD finds the lack of any effort to tender documentation to substantiate these two central components in the claimant's claim for refugee protection causes the panel to question the credibility of the allegations of harm in that claim. The RAD notes that the Appellant had the opportunity to make application to tender additional documents post-hearing in the RPD claim or as new evidence in this appeal.

The RAD notes the Appellant was represented by experienced counsel who ought to have known that these central components of the Appellant's claim would be an issue at the Appellant's hearing. As well, Counsel for the Appellant would be mindful of the obligation and importance of establishing and supporting aspects of the claim as stated in s.11 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules, SOR/2002-228 (the Rules). 11. The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing identity and other elements of the claim. A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents must explain why they were not provided and what steps were taken to obtain them.

In this case, the RAD has reviewed several reasons to doubt the truthfulness and thus the credibility of the claimant. Further to this, the Federal Court has held: "That failure to supply supporting documentation may impact a claimant's credibility, especially if he or she had counsel."11

The RAD does recognize that corroborating evidence is not always required to substantiate a credible claim to refugee protection. However, considering the credibility issues addressed in this claim, as well as the central role that the uncle of the common-law spouse occupies in the Appellant's allegations of harm, as well as the establishment of a viable IFA, corroborating evidence would have been helpful to support the notion that the Appellant's life would be at risk in Nigeria.

On the issue of corroborating evidence, the RAD wishes to note the Federal Court case in Bhagat,12 which states: Corroborating evidence is not always necessary to establish the applicant's subjective fear. The Board, however, determined that in the particular circumstances of this case, corroborating evidence of persecution was expected. An absence of corroborating evidence, then, permitted it to make a negative inference against credibility of the applicant.

The respondent relies on Sheikh13 for its argument that the Board did not err in law when making that conclusion: The concept of "credible evidence" is not, of course, the same as that of the credibility of the applicant, but it is obvious that where the only evidence before a tribunal linking the applicant to his claim is that of the applicant himself (in addition, perhaps, to "country reports" from which nothing about the applicant's claim can be directly deduced), a tribunal's perception that he is not a credible witness effectively amounts to a finding that there is no credible evidence on which the second-level tribunal could allow his claim.

It was apparent as discussed previously that there were a number of important credibility concerns regarding the Appellant's testimony, which leads the RAD to find the failure of the Appellant to supply documentation to support the identity of the common-law spouse's uncle, detracts from the credibility of her allegations. When assessing the findings herein, the RAD agrees with the finding of the RPD in this issue, and the Appellant's argument must fail.

Furthermore, if the RAD were to accept that the appellant's common-law spouse had an uncle in the Benin City police department, no evidence has been adduced that he has any influence or ability to seek the Appellant out in Lagos, a city of 5.2 million. The Appellant has testified that her common-law spouse was able to seek her out at the homes of family or members of her church within 100 kilometres of her home. The RAD notes that the Appellant's testimony and documentation confirm that these are individuals whom her common-law spouse would be familiar with. The RAD finds the ability of the Appellant's persecutor to find them in an obvious location in close proximity does not establish that he has the ability or influence to locate her elsewhere in the country. The RAD further notes that the record indicates the Appellant was able to reside without problems in Lagos for at least two months prior to her departure for Canada.

The RAD has considered the documentary evidence, which suggests that the police in Nigeria are corrupt and that people can be bribed. Furthermore, the RAD has considered that the Appellant does not have a high profile in Nigeria. The RAD finds there is no evidence that the Appellant's common-law spouse has any influence or ability to assist in seeking the Appellant in Lagos, a city of 5.2 million. The RAD further finds that the Appellant has failed to provide persuasive evidence that the common-law spouse has the means or ability to locate and pursue her elsewhere in Nigeria. The RAD has independently assessed the safety of the IFA and finds the Appellant's argument with respect to the inability of the police to protect her elsewhere in Nigeria must fail.

The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that there is not a serious possibility of persecution of the Appellant in Lagos, that her removal to Nigeria would not subject her personally to a risk to her life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture. The Appellant has failed to provide a persuasive explanation as to why she believes she would be discovered and/or harmed in Lagos, and therefore there is no reason to believe, on a balance of probabilities, that she would be harmed.

The RAD considered the reasonableness of the proposed IFA. The test for reasonableness is whether it would be unduly harsh to expect the claimant to move to another, less hostile part of the country before seeking status abroad, as per Thirunavukkarasu.14 This requires an evaluation of the conditions in the IFA as well as the Appellant or similarly-situated persons. Thirunavukkarasu sets a very high threshold for what makes an IFA unreasonable in all the circumstances. The hardship associated with dislocation and relocation is not the kind of undue hardship that renders an IFA unreasonable.15 It is not sufficient for the Appellant to say that he or she does not like the weather there, or that he or she has no friends or relatives there, or that he or she may not be able to find suitable work there.16

The Appellant submits she has no family support and argues the RPD, in its Reasons state that the Appellant must live in hiding to support the notion of an IFA. The RAD finds the submission of the Appellant has little merit.

The RAD has reviewed the record and finds the RPD makes no statement in respect of the Appellant remaining in hiding in Lagos. Nevertheless, the RAD has considered that the fact that an individual has to remain in hiding to avoid problems is not evidence of an IFA17 and that large urban areas cannot be assumed to be an IFA by virtue of their population size alone.18 The RAD's finding of an IFA is not dependent only on the size of Lagos, but is made in consideration of the totality of the evidence. The RAD finds that there is no persuasive evidence to indicate that she would have to live in hiding in Lagos.

The Appellant further submits that it would be difficult for her to live outside of Benin City because she lacks family support. The RAD has considered documentary evidence, which indicates although most Nigerians depend upon their family, relying on immediate and extended family is not the only option. Many Nigerians try to establish other support networks that may complement or in some cases replace the extended family. Examples of such support networks are religious congregations, religious organizations, age grades/sets, political organizations, charities, secret societies and guilds. Many such organizations are expected to aid their members in ways that would be fairly unusual in a western context.

The Appellant has alleged that she is a Christian. The Appellant's own testimony confirms she has received support, shelter and employment through her contacts in her church. For this reason, the RAD is satisfied that the Appellant will have sources of moral and spiritual assistance and support available to her in Nigeria.

The RAD notes that counsel for the Appellant addressed documentary evidence pertaining to IFA, in his submissions to the RPD. The RAD has reviewed and considered these documents. In particular, the United Kingdom Home Office Operational Guidance Note for Nigeria stated that:19 Nigeria is a large country and internal relocation will generally be a viable option for those who fear, or who have experienced ill-treatment at the hands of non-state agents.

The RAD notes that evidence in the record, in particular, the United Kingdom Home Office Operational Guidance Note for Nigeria:20 'WACOL [women's NGO] explained that internal relocation is possible for any adult woman irrespective of whether the case is about FGM, domestic violence or forced marriage. It is possible for adult women to relocate and look for jobs to sustain themselves, however, FGM and forced marriage cases very often involve underage girls. WRAPA (Women's Rights Advancement and Protection Alternative) advised that internal relocation is legally possible, based on the right to freedom of movement as guaranteed by the 1999 Nigerian Constitution, for adult women seeking to escape domestic violence, FGM, forced marriage, and adult women seeking to protect their daughters against FGM. WRAPA considered that internal relocation is a realistic option for such women ... the United Nations Development Fund for Women (UNIFEM) found that in theory, it is not difficult for a woman to relocate within Nigeria and in this way find physical safety...'UNIFEM added that [while seeking to relocate] attractive young, single women, in particular, are very vulnerable to abuse, harassment and trafficking when relocating to another area without economic means or family networks." The same source noted that: According to UNIFEM, the sheer size of the country and its large population means that it would be very difficult for a husband, or other family members, to locate a woman who has escaped FGM, a forced marriage, or is a victim of domestic violence. UNIFEM believed that, should a husband know where his wife has fled to, there is a high risk that he would try to contact her or force her to return home." However, economic constraints may mean that women wishing to relocate may be required to seek assistance from relatives. In addition, social and cultural constraints may leave women stigmatised in their new communities. "BAOBAB further added that young women and/or single women, in particular, who have relocated within Nigeria, are vulnerable to unscrupulous men that may target these women. Some of them might even end up as commercial sex workers.

As previously noted, the record confirms the Appellant has relocated to Lagos, Nigeria prior to her departure to Canada. The RAD has considered that the Appellant has relocated and established herself in a new country, learning a new culture and establishing a support network. The RAD further notes, as previously discussed, the Appellant has an extensive support network available through her church. The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that the Appellant may be able to relocate and find assistance through her support network.

In considering the viability of the IFA, the RAD has given consideration to the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines21 specifically as it relates to IFA. The Guidelines state in part: In determining the reasonableness of a woman's recourse to an internal flight alternative (IFA), decision-makers should consider the ability of women, because of their gender, to travel safely to the IFA and to stay there without facing undue hardship.

The RAD has considered the objective documentary evidence on the difficulty that would be faced by the Appellant as a single woman living in Lagos. The RAD acknowledges that there are challenges faced by women who head their own household in obtaining employment and securing housing and loans. The Appellant has testified that she has previously lived in Lagos as a single woman. The RAD finds, based on the Appellant's level of experience in Nigeria, that she would be able to locate to Lagos and access services there.

The RAD takes note that the Appellant has stated that she has a network of extended family and friends in Nigeria who have already provided her assistance. There is no evidence before the RAD that these individuals will not continue to provide assistance to the Appellant.

The Women's Rights Watch Nigeria project coordinator stated that if women are educated, it is "easier to cope" with running a household without male or family support.22 The same document states that there are more female-headed households in large southern cities than in large northern cities. For this reason, the RAD is satisfied that the Appellant does have access to sources of moral and spiritual assistance and support available to her in the proposed IFAs outside of her family network.

The Appellant does not have a high profile in Nigeria, and the RAD finds that she could live in Lagos. The RAD has previously found that the problems faced by the Appellant with her common-law spouse are local in nature.

The RAD also considered counsel's submissions to the RPD in which he argued that there is no protection against gender-based violence in Nigeria, as well as the Appellant's testimony that the police in Nigeria cannot protect any woman who is abused.

The RAD has considered the profile and influence of the agent of persecution in relation to the IFA. The RAD notes, however, that there is no persuasive evidence in the record, which suggests that the agent of persecution has the ability to access resources of police or any other authorities in order to locate the Appellant if she were to move elsewhere in Nigeria, a country of 150 million people.

Therefore, the RAD finds that the Appellant could live in the proposed IFA city without fear or the need to hide. The RAD notes that Lagos is large and located at a substantial distance from her home in Benin City.
Based on the totality of the evidence, the RAD finds that the record contains sufficient evidence to support a finding that an IFA in Lagos is accessible to the Appellant.

The RAD finds, on a balance of probabilities, that there is not a serious possibility of persecution of the Appellant in Lagos, and her removal to Nigeria would not subject her personally to a risk to her life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture. The Appellant has failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why she believes she would be discovered and/or harmed in Lagos.

The RAD has also considered the Appellant's emotional and mental health in assessing the reasonableness of the IFA. The Appellant has not tendered any documents to indicate that she is currently receiving treatment for any psychological problems addressed in her report from Dr. XXXX. The RAD notes the country condition documents indicate that treatment would be available to the Appellant if she chose to seek treatment in Nigeria. 26.36 The World Health Organisation 2011 Mental Health Atlas for Nigeria noted with regard to the governance arrangements over mental health availability in Nigeria: 'An officially approved mental health policy exists and was approved, or most recently revised, in 1991. Mental health is also specifically mentioned in the general health policy...A mental health plan exists and was approved, or most recently revised, in1991. The mental health plan components include: * Shift of services and resources from mental hospitals to community mental health facilities. * Integration of mental health services into primary care. Dedicated mental health legislation exists and was initiated, or most recently revised, in 1958. Legal provisions concerning mental health are also covered in other laws (e.g., welfare, disability, general health legislation, etc.).' 26.37 The same source noted that information on mental health and mental hospital expenditures by the government health department were not available. The report went on to list mental health care delivery in the country as follows: 'Primary Care ... Prescription regulations authorize primary health care doctors to prescribe and/or to continue prescription of psychotherapeutic medicines but with restrictions. Similarly, the department of health authorizes primary health care nurses to prescribe and/or to continue prescription of psychotherapeutic medicines, with restrictions. Official policy enables primary health care nurses to independently diagnose and treat mental disorders within the primary care system.23

Once the issue of an internal flight alternative is raised, the onus is on the refugee claimant to show that the option does not exist by establishing that either of the two tests cited in Rasaratnam24 criteria is not met. The Federal Court of Appeal in Thirunavukkarasu stated that an applicant need only show that there is a serious possibility of being persecuted in the new location or that their removal to Nigeria would not subject them personally to a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture. The RAD finds that the Appellant has failed to show that the IFA option is not available.

The RAD, in assessing the reasonableness of the IFA for the Appellant, has considered the application of the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines25 specifically as it relates to IFA, the Appellant's psychological and emotional health as well as her testimony and the documentary evidence. Given the finding above that the Appellant has an internal flight alternative in Nigeria, the RAD finds that the Appellant does not face a serious possibility of persecution there and also finds that her removal to Nigeria would not subject her personally to a risk to life, or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture. Summary

The Appellant has failed to provide a reasonable explanation as to why she believes she would be discovered and/or harmed at the IFA location, and therefore there is no reason to believe, on a balance of probabilities, that she would be harmed.
The problem faced by the Appellant with her common-law spouse is local in nature.
The Appellant has not provided any persuasive evidence how her common-law spouse would come to know that she was living elsewhere in Nigeria.
The Appellant could live in the city proposed as an IFA. Disposition
The RAD finds that there is an IFA for the Appellant, and since IFA is a determinative issue, the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

Pursuant to ss. 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the determination of the RPD and dismisses the appeal.
